name: Memory Safety & Exploitation
description: Memory-corruption bugs, exploitation techniques, and mitigations (ASLR, CFI, sanitizers).
narrative:
The earliest papers in this list mark a turning point where memory safety research collided with hardware microarchitecture. The headline work, "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (2018), showed that the CPU's own out-of-order execution could be coaxed into leaking kernel memory across the isolation boundary that operating systems depend on, fundamentally changing what "memory safety" had to account for. Alongside it, 2018 saw a wave of practical exploitation tooling: "FUZE: Towards Facilitating Exploit Generation for Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities" (2018) automated the hard step of turning a kernel use-after-free into a working exploit, while "IMIX: In-Process Memory Isolation EXtension" (2018) and "Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading" (2018) pushed the defensive side toward finer-grained isolation and shrinking the attack surface.

Through 2019 and 2020 the field broadened from classic userland and kernel bugs into new execution environments and trust domains. "TeeRex: Discovery and Exploitation of Memory Corruption Vulnerabilities in SGX Enclaves" (2020) carried memory-corruption hunting into Intel SGX enclaves, showing that hardware-backed trusted execution was not immune, and "Everything Old is New Again: Binary Security of WebAssembly" (2020) demonstrated that a modern, supposedly safe compilation target reintroduced old corruption primitives. This period reflects a recurring theme in the area: every new abstraction layer inherits familiar memory bugs in unfamiliar clothing.

By 2021 and 2022 the frontier shifted decisively toward the hardware substrate and its mitigations. "SMASH: Synchronized Many-sided Rowhammer Attacks from JavaScript" (2021) defeated in-DRAM Target Row Refresh defenses straight from a web page, while "Nyx: Greybox Hypervisor Fuzzing using Fast Snapshots and Affine Types" (2021) advanced fuzzing into the hypervisor layer where the strongest isolation boundaries live. Most tellingly, "Branch History Injection: On the Effectiveness of Hardware Mitigations Against Cross-Privilege Spectre-v2 Attacks" (2022) showed that the hardware countermeasures deployed after the original transient-execution attacks were themselves bypassable. Taken together, the trajectory runs from automating exploitation of software bugs, through extending the hunt into trusted and managed runtimes, to an ongoing cat-and-mouse contest over the physical and microarchitectural mitigations meant to contain these attacks.
